      <content name="title"><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt3">Chronic</span> <span class="qt4">Obstructive</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">Pulmonary</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Disease</span></span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>?<p><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span><span class="qt3"> (chronic</span> <span class="qt4">obstructive</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">pulmonary</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">disease</span></span>) is a group of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">lung</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">diseases</span></span> that make it hard to breathe and get worse over time.</p><p>Normally, the airways and air sacs in your <span class="qt0">lungs</span> are elastic or stretchy. When you breathe in, the airways bring air to the air sacs. The air sacs fill up with air, like a small balloon. When you breathe out, the air sacs deflate, and the air goes out. If you have <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>, less air flows in and out of your airways because of one or more problems:</p><ul><li>The airways and air sacs in your <span class="qt0">lungs</span> become less elastic</li><li>The walls between many of the air sacs are destroyed</li><li>The walls of the airways become thick and inflamed</li><li>The airways make more mucus than usual and can become clogged</li></ul>What are the types of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>?<p><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span> includes two main types:</p><ul><li>Emphysema affects the air sacs in your <span class="qt0">lungs</span>, as well as the walls between them. They become damaged and are less elastic.</li><li><span class="qt3">Chronic</span> bronchitis, in which the lining of your airways is constantly irritated and inflamed. This causes the lining to swell and make mucus.</li></ul><p>Most people with <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span> have both emphysema and <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis, but how severe each type is can be different from person to person.</p>What causes <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>?<p>The cause of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span> is usually long-term exposure to irritants that damage your <span class="qt0">lungs</span> and airways. In the United States, cigarette smoke is the main cause. Pipe, cigar, and other types of tobacco smoke can also cause <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>, especially if you inhale them.</p><p>Exposure to other inhaled irritants can contribute to <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>. These include secondhand smoke, air pollution, and chemical fumes or dusts from the environment or workplace.</p><p>Rarely, a genetic condition called alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency can play a role in causing <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>.</p>Who is more likely to develop <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>?<p>Certain factors make you more likely to develop <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>. These include:</p><ul><li>Smoking. This is the main risk factor. Up to 75% of people who have <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span> smoke or used to smoke.</li><li>Long-term exposure to other <span class="qt0">lung</span> irritants, such as secondhand smoke, air pollution, and chemical fumes and dusts from the environment or workplace</li><li>Age. Most people who have <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span> are at least 40 years old when their symptoms begin.</li><li>Genetics. This includes alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, which is a genetic condition. Also, smokers who get <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span> are more likely to get it if they have a family history of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>.</li><li>Asthma. People who have asthma have more risk of developing <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span> than people who don't have asthma. But most people with asthma will not get <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>?<p>At first, you may have no symptoms or only mild symptoms. As the <span class="qt1">disease</span> gets worse, your symptoms usually become more severe. They can include:</p><ul><li>Frequent coughing or a cough that produces a lot of mucus</li><li>Wheezing  or a whistling or squeaky sound when you breathe</li><li>Shortness of breath, especially with physical activity</li><li>Tightness in your chest</li><li>Fatigue</li></ul><p>Some people with <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span> get frequent respiratory infections such as colds and the flu. In severe cases, <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span> can cause weight loss, weakness in your lower muscles, and swelling in your ankles, feet, and legs.</p>How is <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span> diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>, your health care provider may:</p><ul><li>Ask about your medical history, which includes asking about your symptoms</li><li>Ask about your family history</li><li>Ask if you have ever smoked or been exposed to secondhand smoke and other <span class="qt0">lung</span> irritants </li><li>Order various tests, such as <span class="qt0">lung</span> function tests, a chest x-ray or CT scan</li><li>Order blood tests, which may include an arterial blood gas test or an alpha-1 antitrypsin test</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>?<p>There is no cure for <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>. However, treatments can help with symptoms, slow the progress of the <span class="qt1">disease</span>, and improve your ability to stay active. There are also treatments to prevent or treat complications of the <span class="qt1">disease</span>. Treatments include:</p><ul><li>Lifestyle changes, such as:<ul><li>Quitting smoking if you are a smoker. This is the most important step you can take to treat <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>.</li><li>Avoiding secondhand smoke and places where you might breathe in other <span class="qt0">lung</span> irritants.</li><li>Following an eating plan that meets your nutritional needs.</li><li>Increasing your physical activity as your condition allows. Ask your provider about how much physical activity you can do. Physical activity can strengthen the muscles that help you breathe and improve your overall wellness.</li></ul></li><li>Medicines, such as:<ul><li>Bronchodilators, which relax the muscles around your airways. This helps open your airways and makes breathing easier. Most bronchodilators are taken through an inhaler. In more severe cases, the inhaler may also contain steroids to reduce inflammation.</li><li>Vaccines for the flu and pneumococcal pneumonia, since people with <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span> are at higher risk for serious problems from these <span class="qt1">diseases</span></li><li>Antibiotics if you get a bacterial <span class="qt0">lung</span> infection</li><li>Biologics, which are a type of medicine made from living sources, such as cells, tissues, and proteins. A biologic medicine may reduce inflammation in certain types of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span></li></ul></li><li>Oxygen therapy, if you have severe <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span> and low levels of oxygen in your blood. Oxygen therapy can help you breathe better. You may need extra oxygen all the time or only at certain times.</li><li><span class="qt0">Pulmonary</span> rehabilitation, which is a program that helps improve the well-being of people who have <span class="qt3">chronic</span> breathing problems. It may include:<ul><li>An exercise program</li><li><span class="qt1">Disease</span> management training</li><li>Nutritional counseling</li><li>Psychological counseling</li></ul></li><li>Surgery, usually as a last resort for people who have severe symptoms that have not gotten better with medicines:
	<ul><li>For <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span> that is mainly related to emphysema, there are surgeries that: 
			<ul><li>Remove damaged <span class="qt0">lung</span> tissue.</li><li>Remove large air spaces (bullae) that can form when air sacs are destroyed. The bullae can interfere with breathing.</li></ul>
		</li><li>For severe <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>, some people may need a <span class="qt0">lung</span> transplant.</li></ul></li></ul><p>If you have <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>, it's important to know when and where to get help for your symptoms. You should get emergency care if you have severe symptoms, such as trouble catching your breath or talking. Call your provider if your symptoms are getting worse or if you have signs of an infection, such as a fever.</p>Can <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span> be prevented?<p>Since smoking causes most cases of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>, the best way to prevent it is not to smoke. It's also important to try to avoid <span class="qt0">lung</span> irritants such as secondhand smoke, air pollution, chemical fumes, and dusts.</p><p>NIH: National Heart, <span class="qt0">Lung</span>, and Blood Institute</p></content>

      <content name="title"><span class="qt3">Chronic</span> Bronchitis</content>

      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis?<p><span class="qt3">Chronic</span> bronchitis is a type of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span><span class="qt3"> (chronic</span> <span class="qt4">obstructive</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">pulmonary</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">disease). </span></span><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span> is a group of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">lung</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">diseases</span></span> that make it hard to breathe and get worse over time. The other main type of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span> is emphysema. Most people with <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span> have both emphysema and <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis, but how severe each type is can be different from person to person.</p><p><span class="qt3">Chronic</span> bronchitis is inflammation (swelling) and irritation of the bronchial tubes. These tubes are the airways that carry air to and from the air sacs in your <span class="qt0">lungs</span>. The irritation of the tubes causes mucus to build up. This mucus and the swelling of the tubes make it harder for your <span class="qt0">lungs</span> to move oxygen in and carbon dioxide out of your body.</p>What causes <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis?<p>The cause of <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis is usually long-term exposure to irritants that damage your <span class="qt0">lungs</span> and airways. In the United States, cigarette smoke is the main cause. Pipe, cigar, and other types of tobacco smoke can also cause <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis, especially if you inhale them.</p><p>Exposure to other inhaled irritants can contribute to <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis. These include secondhand smoke, air pollution, and chemical fumes or dusts from the environment or workplace.</p><p>Rarely, a genetic condition called alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency can play a role in causing <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis.</p>Who is at risk for <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis?<p>The risk factors for <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis include:</p><ul><li>Smoking. This the main risk factor. Up to 75% of people who have <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis smoke or used to smoke.</li><li>Long-term exposure to other <span class="qt0">lung</span> irritants, such as secondhand smoke, air pollution, and chemical fumes and dusts from the environment or workplace.</li><li>Age. Most people who have <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis are at least 40 years old when their symptoms begin.</li><li>Genetics. This includes alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, which is a genetic condition. Also, smokers who get <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis are more likely to get it if they have a family history of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis?<p>At first, you may have no symptoms or only mild symptoms. As the <span class="qt1">disease</span> gets worse, your symptoms usually become more severe. They can include:</p><ul><li>Frequent coughing or a cough that produces a lot mucus</li><li>Wheezing</li><li>A whistling or squeaky sound when you breathe</li><li>Shortness of breath, especially with physical activity</li><li>Tightness in your chest</li></ul><p>Some people with <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis get frequent respiratory infections such as colds and the flu. In severe cases, <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis can cause weight loss, weakness in your lower muscles, and swelling in your ankles, feet, or legs.</p>How is <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis diagnosed?<p>Your health care provider may use many tools to make a diagnosis:</p><ul><li>A medical history, which includes asking about your symptoms</li><li>A family history</li><li>Various tests, such as <span class="qt0">lung</span> function tests, a chest x-ray or CT scan, and blood tests</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis?<p>There is no cure for <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis. However, treatments can help with symptoms, slow the progress of the <span class="qt1">disease</span>, and improve your ability to stay active. There are also treatments to prevent or treat complications of the <span class="qt1">disease</span>. Treatments include:</p><ul><li>Lifestyle changes, such as
	<ul><li>Quitting smoking if you are a smoker. This is the most important step you can take to treat <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis.</li><li>Avoiding secondhand smoke and places where you might breathe in other <span class="qt0">lung</span> irritants</li><li>Ask your health care provider for an eating plan that will meet your nutritional needs. Also ask about how much physical activity you can do. Physical activity can strengthen the muscles that help you breathe and improve your overall wellness.</li></ul></li><li>Medicines, such as
	<ul><li>Bronchodilators, which relax the muscles around your airways. This helps open your airways and makes breathing easier. Most bronchodilators are taken through an inhaler. In more severe cases, the inhaler may also contain steroids to reduce inflammation.</li><li>Vaccines for the flu and pneumococcal pneumonia, since people with <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis are at higher risk for serious problems from these <span class="qt1">diseases</span>.</li><li>Antibiotics if you get a bacterial or viral <span class="qt0">lung</span> infection</li></ul></li><li>Oxygen therapy, if you have severe <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis and low levels of oxygen in your blood. Oxygen therapy can help you breathe better. You may need extra oxygen all the time or only at certain times.</li><li><span class="qt0">Pulmonary</span> rehabilitation, which is a program that helps improve the well-being of people who have <span class="qt3">chronic</span> breathing problems. It may include</li><ul><li>An exercise program</li><li><span class="qt1">Disease</span> management training</li><li>Nutritional counseling</li><li>Psychological counseling</li></ul><li>A <span class="qt0">lung</span> transplant, as a last resort for people who have severe symptoms that have not gotten better with medicines</li></ul><p>If you have <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis, it's important to know when and where to get help for your symptoms. You should get emergency care if you have severe symptoms, such as trouble catching your breath or talking. Call your health care provider if your symptoms are getting worse or if you have signs of an infection, such as a fever.</p>Can <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis be prevented?<p>Since smoking causes most cases of <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis, the best way to prevent it is to not smoke. It's also important to try to avoid <span class="qt0">lung</span> irritants such as secondhand smoke, air pollution, chemical fumes, and dusts.</p><p>


</p><p>NIH: National Heart, <span class="qt0">Lung</span>, and Blood Institute</p></content>

      <content name="title">Emphysema</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Pulmonary</span> Emphysema</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is emphysema?<p>Emphysema is a type of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span><span class="qt3"> (chronic</span> <span class="qt4">obstructive</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">pulmonary</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">disease). </span></span><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span> is a group of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">lung</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">diseases</span></span> that make it hard to breathe and get worse over time. The other main type of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span><span class="qt3"> is chronic</span> bronchitis. Most people with <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span> have both emphysema and <span class="qt3">chronic</span> bronchitis, but how severe each type is can be different from person to person.</p><p>Emphysema affects the air sacs in your <span class="qt0">lungs</span>. Normally, these sacs are elastic or stretchy. When you breathe in, each air sac fills up with air, like a small balloon. When you breathe out, the air sacs deflate, and the air goes out.</p><p>In emphysema, the walls between many of the air sacs in the <span class="qt0">lungs</span> are damaged. This causes the air sacs to lose their shape and become floppy. The damage also can destroy the walls of the air sacs, leading to fewer and larger air sacs instead of many tiny ones. This makes it harder for your <span class="qt0">lungs</span> to move oxygen in and carbon dioxide out of your body.</p>What causes emphysema?<p>The cause of emphysema is usually long-term exposure to irritants that damage your <span class="qt0">lungs</span> and the airways. In the United States, cigarette smoke is the main cause. Pipe, cigar, and other types of tobacco smoke can also cause emphysema, especially if you inhale them.</p><p>Exposure to other inhaled irritants can contribute to emphysema. These include secondhand smoke, air pollution, and chemical fumes or dusts from the environment or workplace.</p><p>Rarely, a genetic condition called alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency can play a role in causing emphysema.</p>Who is at risk for emphysema?<p>The risk factors for emphysema include:</p><ul><li>Smoking. This the main risk factor. Up to 75% of people who have emphysema smoke or used to smoke.</li><li>Long-term exposure to other <span class="qt0">lung</span> irritants, such as secondhand smoke, air pollution, and chemical fumes and dusts from the environment or workplace.</li><li>Age. Most people who have emphysema are at least 40 years old when their symptoms begin.</li><li>Genetics. This includes alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, which is a genetic condition. Also, smokers who get emphysema are more likely to get it if they have a family history of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span>.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of emphysema?<p>At first, you may have no symptoms or only mild symptoms. As the <span class="qt1">disease</span> gets worse, your symptoms usually become more severe. They can include:</p><ul><li>Frequent coughing or wheezing</li><li>A cough that produces a lot mucus</li><li>Shortness of breath, especially with physical activity</li><li>A whistling or squeaky sound when you breathe</li><li>Tightness in your chest</li></ul><p>Some people with emphysema get frequent respiratory infections such as colds and the flu. In severe cases, emphysema can cause weight loss, weakness in your lower muscles, and swelling in your ankles, feet, or legs.</p>How is emphysema diagnosed?<p>Your health care provider may use many tools to make a diagnosis:</p><ul><li>A medical history, which includes asking about your symptoms</li><li>A family history</li><li>Other tests, such as <span class="qt0">lung</span> function tests, a chest x-ray or CT scan, and blood tests</li></ul>What are the treatments for emphysema?<p>There is no cure for emphysema. However, treatments can help with symptoms, slow the progress of the <span class="qt1">disease</span>, and improve your ability to stay active. There are also treatments to prevent or treat complications of the <span class="qt1">disease</span>. Treatments include:</p><ul><li>Lifestyle changes, such as
	<ul><li>Quitting smoking if you are a smoker. This is the most important step you can take to treat emphysema.</li><li>Avoiding secondhand smoke and places where you might breathe in other <span class="qt0">lung</span> irritants</li><li>Ask your health care provider for an eating plan that will meet your nutritional needs. Also ask about how much physical activity you can do. Physical activity can strengthen the muscles that help you breathe and improve your overall wellness.</li></ul></li><li>Medicines, such as
	<ul><li>Bronchodilators, which relax the muscles around your airways. This helps open your airways and makes breathing easier. Most bronchodilators are taken through an inhaler. In more severe cases, the inhaler may also contain steroids to reduce inflammation.</li><li>Vaccines for the flu and pneumococcal pneumonia, since people with emphysema are at higher risk for serious problems from these <span class="qt1">diseases</span></li><li>Antibiotics if you get a bacterial or viral <span class="qt0">lung</span> infection</li></ul></li><li>Oxygen therapy, if you have severe emphysema and low levels of oxygen in your blood. Oxygen therapy can help you breathe better. You may need extra oxygen all the time or only at certain times.</li><li><span class="qt0">Pulmonary</span> rehabilitation, which is a program that helps improve the well-being of people who have <span class="qt3">chronic</span> breathing problems. It may include
	<ul><li>An exercise program</li><li><span class="qt1">Disease</span> management training</li><li>Nutritional counseling</li><li>Psychological counseling</li></ul></li><li>Surgery, usually as a last resort for people who have severe symptoms that have not gotten better with medicines. There are surgeries to 
	<ul><li>Remove damaged <span class="qt0">lung</span> tissue</li><li>Remove large air spaces (bullae) that can form when air sacs are destroyed. The bullae can interfere with breathing.</li><li>Do a <span class="qt0">lung</span> transplant. This is might be an option if you have very severe emphysema.</li></ul></li></ul><p>If you have emphysema, it's important to know when and where to get help for your symptoms. You should get emergency care if you have severe symptoms, such as trouble catching your breath or talking. Call your health care provider if your symptoms are getting worse or if you have signs of an infection, such as a fever.</p>Can emphysema be prevented?<p>Since smoking causes most cases of emphysema, the best way to prevent it is to not smoke. It's also important to try to avoid <span class="qt0">lung</span> irritants such as secondhand smoke, air pollution, chemical fumes, and dusts.</p><p>NIH: National Heart, <span class="qt0">Lung</span>, and Blood Institute</p></content>

      <content name="title">Heart Failure</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">CHF</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Cardiac Failure</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Congestive Heart Failure</content>

      <content name="altTitle">Left-sided heart failure</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Right-sided heart failure</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is heart failure?<p>Heart failure means that your heart can't pump enough oxygen-rich blood to meet your body's needs. Heart failure doesn't mean that your heart has stopped or is about to stop beating. But without enough blood flow, your organs may not work well, which can cause serious problems.</p><p>Heart failure can affect one or both sides of your heart:</p><ul><li>With right-sided heart failure, your heart is too weak to pump enough blood to your <span class="qt0">lungs</span> to get oxygen.</li><li>With left-sided heart failure, your heart can't pump enough oxygen-rich blood out to your body. This happens when the left side of your heart becomes either:
	<ul><li>Too weak to pump enough blood.</li><li>Too thick or stiff to relax and fill with enough blood.</li></ul></li></ul><p>Left-sided heart failure is more common than right-sided heart failure.</p>What causes heart failure?<p>Heart failure can start suddenly after a medical condition or injury damages your heart muscle. But in most cases, heart failure develops slowly from long-term medical conditions.</p><p>Conditions that can cause heart failure include:</p><ul><li>Arrhythmia (a problem with the rate or rhythm of your heartbeat)</li><li>Cardiomyopathy</li><li>Congenital heart defects or other types of heart <span class="qt1">diseases</span> that you are born with</li><li>Coronary artery <span class="qt1">disease</span></li><li>Endocarditis</li><li>Heart attack</li><li>Heart valve <span class="qt1">diseases</span></li><li>High blood pressure</li><li>A blood clot in your <span class="qt0">lung</span></li><li>Diabetes</li><li>Certain severe <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">lung</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">diseases</span></span>, such as <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span><span class="qt3"> (chronic</span> <span class="qt4">obstructive</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">pulmonary</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">disease</span></span>)</li><li>Obesity</li></ul><p>Over time, left-sided heart failure can lead to right-sided heart failure.</p>Who is more likely to develop heart failure?<p>Heart failure can happen at any age. It happens to both men and women, but men often develop it at a younger age than women.  Your chance of developing heart failure increases if:</p><ul><li>You're 65 years old or older. Aging can weaken and stiffen your heart muscle.</li><li>Your family health history includes relatives who have or have had heart failure.</li><li>You have changes in your genes that affect your heart tissue.</li><li>You have habits that can harm your heart, including:
	<ul><li>Smoking</li><li>Eating foods high in fat, cholesterol, and sodium (salt)</li><li>Having an inactive lifestyle</li><li>Alcohol use disorder (AUD)</li><li>Illegal drug use</li></ul></li><li>You have other medical conditions that can affect your heart, including: 
	<ul><li>Any heart or blood vessel conditions, including high blood pressure</li><li>Serious <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">lung</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">diseases</span></span></li><li>Infection, such as HIV or COVID-19</li><li>Obesity</li><li>Diabetes</li><li>Sleep apnea</li><li><span class="qt3">Chronic</span> kidney <span class="qt1">disease</span></li><li>Anemia</li><li>Thyroid <span class="qt1">disease</span></li><li>Iron overload <span class="qt1">disease</span></li><li>Cancer treatments that can harm your heart, such as radiation and chemotherapy</li></ul></li><li>You are African American. African Americans are more likely to develop heart failure and have more serious cases at younger ages than people of other races. Factors such as stigma, discrimination, income, education, and geographic region can also affect their risk of heart failure.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of heart failure?<p>The symptoms of heart failure depend on which side of your heart is affected and how serious your condition has become.  Most symptoms are caused by reduced blood flow to your organs and fluid buildup in your body.</p><p>Fluid buildup happens because the flow of blood through your heart is too slow. As a result, blood backs up in the vessels that return the blood to your heart. Fluid may leak from the blood vessels and collect in the tissues of your body, causing swelling (edema) and other problems.</p><p>Symptoms of heart failure may include:</p><ul><li>Feeling short of breath (like you can't get enough air) when you do things like climbing stairs. This may be one of the first symptoms you notice.</li><li>Fatigue or weakness even after rest.</li><li>Coughing.</li><li>Swelling and weight gain from fluid in your ankles, lower legs, or abdomen (belly).</li><li>Difficulty sleeping when lying flat.</li><li>Nausea and loss of appetite.</li><li>Swelling in the veins of your neck.</li><li>Needing to urinate (pee) often.</li></ul><p>At first you may have no symptoms or mild symptoms. As the <span class="qt1">disease</span> gets worse, your symptoms will usually bother you more.</p>What other problems does heart failure cause?<p>Fluid buildup and reduced blood flow to your organs can lead to serious problems, including:</p><ul><li>Breathing problems from fluid in and around your <span class="qt0">lungs</span> (also called congestive heart failure)</li><li>Kidney or liver damage, including cirrhosis</li><li>Malnutrition if fluid buildup makes eating uncomfortable or if your stomach doesn't get enough blood flow to digest food properly</li><li>Other heart conditions, such as irregular heartbeat and sudden cardiac arrest</li><li><span class="qt0">Pulmonary</span> hypertension</li></ul>How is heart failure diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have heart failure, your health care provider will</p><p> 
</p><ul><li>Ask about your medical history, including your symptoms</li><li>Ask about your family health history, including relatives who have had heart failure</li><li>Do a physical exam</li><li>Likely run heart tests and blood tests, including a brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) test</li></ul><p>In some cases, your provider may refer you to a cardiologist (a doctor who specializes in heart <span class="qt1">diseases</span>) for tests, diagnosis, and care.</p>What are the treatments for heart failure?<p>Your treatment will depend on the type of heart failure you have and how serious it is. There's no cure for heart failure. But treatment can help you live longer with fewer symptoms.</p><p>Even with treatment, heart failure usually gets worse over time, so you'll likely need treatment for the rest of your life.</p><p>Most treatment plans include:</p><ul><li>Taking medicine</li><li>Eating less sodium and drinking less liquid to control fluid buildup</li><li>Making other changes, such as quitting smoking, managing stress, and getting as much physical activity as your provider recommends</li><li>Treating any conditions that may make heart failure worse</li></ul><p>You may need heart surgery if:</p><ul><li>You have a congenital heart defect or damage to your heart that can be fixed.</li><li>The left side of your heart is getting weaker and putting a device in your chest could help. Devices include:
	<ul><li>An implantable cardioverter defibrillator.</li><li>A biventricular pacemaker (cardiac resynchronization therapy).</li><li>A mechanical heart pump (a ventricular assist device (VAD) or a total artificial heart).</li></ul>
</li><li>Your heart doctor recommends a heart transplant because your heart failure is life-threatening and nothing else is helping.</li></ul><p>As part of your treatment, you'll need to pay close attention to your symptoms, because heart failure can worsen suddenly. Your provider may suggest a cardiac rehabilitation program to help you learn how to manage your condition.</p>Can heart failure be prevented?<p>You may be able to prevent or delay heart failure if you:</p><ul><li>Work with your provider to manage any health conditions that increase your risk of developing heart failure</li><li>Make healthy changes in your eating, exercise, and other daily habits to help prevent heart <span class="qt1">disease</span></li></ul><p>NIH: National Heart, <span class="qt0">Lung</span>, and Blood Institute</p></content>

      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Pulmonary</span> Hypertension</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Cor Pulmonale</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Hypertension, <span class="qt0">Pulmonary</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Primary <span class="qt0">Pulmonary</span> Hypertension</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Pulmonary</span> Arterial Hypertension</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> hypertension? <p><span class="qt0">Pulmonary</span> hypertension, sometimes called PH, is a serious condition that affects the blood vessels in the <span class="qt0">lungs</span>. It develops when the blood pressure in your <span class="qt0">lungs</span> is higher than normal.</p><p>Your heart pumps blood to your <span class="qt0">lungs</span> so they can add oxygen to the blood. The blood goes back to your heart. From there, it travels to the rest of your body so that your tissues can get the oxygen that they need.</p><p>The blood moves from your heart to your <span class="qt0">lungs</span> through blood vessels called <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> arteries. If the <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> arteries become damaged, narrowed, or blocked, the blood does not flow through them as well. This can increase the blood pressure in the arteries and cause <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> hypertension.</p><p>There are different types of <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> hypertension, including <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> arterial hypertension (PAH). The different types are based on what caused the <span class="qt1">disease</span>.</p>What causes <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> hypertension?<p><span class="qt0">Pulmonary</span> hypertension can develop on its own or be caused by another condition. Sometimes the cause is unknown or is not clear.</p><p>Some of the possible causes include:</p><ul><li>Heart <span class="qt1">diseases</span>, including left-sided heart failure and congenital heart <span class="qt1">disease</span></li><li><span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">Lung</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">diseases</span></span> such as <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">COPD</span></span></span></span></span><span class="qt3"> (chronic</span> <span class="qt4">obstructive</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">pulmonary</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">disease</span></span>), interstitial <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">lung</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">disease</span></span>, emphysema, and sleep apnea</li><li>Other medical conditions such as:
  <ul><li>Liver <span class="qt1">diseases</span></li><li>Sickle cell <span class="qt1">disease</span></li><li><span class="qt0">Pulmonary</span> embolism (blood clots in the <span class="qt0">lungs</span>)</li><li>Connective tissue disorders like scleroderma</li></ul>
</li></ul>Who is more likely to develop <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> hypertension? <p>Certain factors can make you more likely to develop <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> hypertension, such as:</p><ul><li>Your age. The risk increases as you get older. The condition is usually diagnosed between ages 30 and 60.</li><li>Your environment. Being exposed to asbestos or having certain infections caused by parasites can raise your risk.</li><li>Your family history and genetics. Certain genetic disorders, such as Down syndrome, congenital heart <span class="qt1">disease</span>, and Gaucher <span class="qt1">disease</span>, can raise your risk of <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> hypertension. So can a family history of blood clots.</li><li>Your lifestyle habits.Smoking and illegal drug use can raise your risk of developing <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> hypertension.</li><li>Certain medicines. For example, some medicines used to treat cancer and depression can make you more likely to develop <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> hypertension.</li><li>Your sex. <span class="qt0">Pulmonary</span> hypertension is more common in women than in men.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> hypertension?<p>The symptoms of <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> hypertension are sometimes hard to recognize and are similar to the symptoms of other medical conditions. So sometimes it can take years for someone to get diagnosed with <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> hypertension.</p><p>The symptoms of <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> hypertension may include:</p><ul><li>Shortness of breath</li><li>Chest pain or pressure</li><li>Dizziness that may lead to fainting</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Swelling of the abdomen, legs, or feet</li><li>Heart palpitations (the feeling that your heart is pounding or beating too fast)</li></ul>What other problems can <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> hypertension cause?<p><span class="qt0">Pulmonary</span> hypertension can get worse over time and lead to serious problems, including:</p><ul><li>Anemia, which can cause your body to not get enough oxygen-rich blood</li><li>Arrhythmias, problems with the rate or rhythm of your heartbeat</li><li>Blood clots in the <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> arteries</li><li>Bleeding in the <span class="qt0">lungs</span></li><li>Heart failure</li><li>Liver damage</li><li>Pericardial effusion, a collection of fluid around the heart</li><li>Serious pregnancy complications</li></ul>How is <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> hypertension diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> hypertension, your health care provider:</p><ul><li>Will ask about your medical history and symptoms</li><li>Will do a physical exam, which may include checking your blood oxygen, listening to your heart and <span class="qt0">lungs</span>, and checking your blood pressure</li><li>Will likely order some tests, such as:
  <ul><li>Blood tests to look for blood clots, stress on the heart, or anemia</li><li>Heart imaging tests, such as a cardiac MRI</li><li><span class="qt0">Lung</span> imaging tests, such as chest x-ray</li><li>An electrocardiogram (ECG or EKG)</li></ul>
</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> hypertension?<p>Often there is no cure for <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> hypertension, but treatments can help manage your symptoms. Your provider will work with you to come up with a treatment plan. It will be based on your needs and the cause of the <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> hypertension. The plan may include:</p><ul><li>Healthy lifestyle changes, such as:
  <ul><li>Healthy eating, which includes eating less salt</li><li>Regular physical activity, which may be done through <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> rehabilitation</li></ul>
</li><li>Medicines, such as:
  <ul><li>Blood thinners</li><li>Medicines to control the rate blood is pumped throughout the body</li><li>Medicines to relax blood vessels and allow the blood to flow better</li><li>Medicine to reduce swelling (diuretics)</li></ul>
</li><li>Oxygen therapy</li><li>Procedures to reduce pressure in the heart or <span class="qt0">pulmonary</span> artery</li><li>In some severe cases, a <span class="qt0">lung</span> transplant</li></ul><p>NIH: National Heart, <span class="qt0">Lung</span>, and Blood Institute</p></content>
